title: Why our IQ levels are higher than our grandparents' | James Flynn
summary: Moral philosopher James Flynn explains the Flynn effect, the steady rise of IQ scores across the 20th century. He argues the shift reflects a move toward abstract, hypothetical thinking as cognitively demanding professions grew.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a clear explanation of why generations think differently and why IQ scores have risen.

title: CIA Officer in Charge of Taking Down the AQ Khan Network | James Lawler | Ep. 125
summary: A long Team House podcast interview with James Lawler, a former CIA operations officer who led counterproliferation work against the A.Q. Khan nuclear network. He discusses HUMINT, WMD and how such operations were run.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an in-depth look at the mechanics of intelligence work from a veteran who ran a nonproliferation operation.

title: Information, Evolution, and intelligent Design - With Daniel Dennett
summary: Daniel Dennett gives a Royal Institution talk toward a unified theory of information, tying together evolution, learning and engineering. He argues that design can arise bottom-up through small steps without a designer.
why_hn: Recommended for its account of competence without comprehension, relevant to evolution and to debates about AI.

title: A visual guide to Bayesian thinking
summary: Julia Galef uses pictures to explain Bayes' rule, then tells three personal stories showing how she applies it to improve her thinking.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a short, accessible intro to Bayesian reasoning and priors.

title: Neil deGrasse Tyson - We Stopped Dreaming (Episode 1)
summary: A short, music-driven video built from Neil deGrasse Tyson's remarks on why advancing the space frontier matters, contrasting NASA's small budget with war spending and stressing inspiration.
why_hn: Recommended to anyone asking whether space exploration is worth the cost.

title: Thinking, Fast and Slow | Daniel Kahneman | Talks at Google
summary: Daniel Kahneman's Talks at Google lecture on his book Thinking, Fast and Slow, covering System 1 and System 2 thinking and the psychology of judgment and decision making.
why_hn: Recommended as a one-hour substitute for the book's opening chapters for those short on time.

title: James Mickens on JavaScript
summary: James Mickens delivers his comedic rant about JavaScript and web programming, in his usual dry, hyperbolic style. It includes his account of learning the language from the O'Reilly Definitive Guide.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a hilarious talk by a beloved speaker, and also uses it to jab at JavaScript's quirks.

title: CppCon 2016: Dan Saks “extern c: Talking to C Programmers about C++”
hn_categories: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
summary: Dan Saks's CppCon 2016 talk on why C programmers resist C++ and how to talk to them about it. He argues that persuasion rarely works by arguing and examines the culture gap between the two communities.
why_hn: Recommended in C versus C++ and embedded threads as the expert view on adoption and persuasion.

title: Oswald Acted Alone: JFK Assassination Solved (Part 1 of 2)
summary: The first part of a long two-part video series by historian Sean Munger arguing, with citations, that Lee Harvey Oswald assassinated President Kennedy and acted alone. It goes through the provable historical facts and addresses conspiracy theories.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as the most exhaustive, well-sourced rebuttal of JFK conspiracy theories, often when new assassination claims surface.

title: The Why, What, and How of Pinning in Rust
hn_categories: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
summary: Jon Gjengset's long live-coding stream explains Rust's Pin and Unpin types: why they exist, how they work, and how they connect to futures and async/await. It also covers moving from pre-pinning code to the new model.
why_hn: HN treats it as the definitive resource for understanding Pin semantics and lists it among async Rust learning materials.

title: 1,500 Slot Machines Walk into a Bar: Adventures in Quantity Over Quality
summary: In this 2019 GDC talk, Alex Schwartz and Ziba Scott explain how they flooded the app stores with over 1,500 auto-generated slot machine games to find the lowest bar for success. They tour the dark side of the mobile app market.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a hilarious account of mass-produced app store shovelware and cite it in threads on spam and low-quality content.

title: Prius Hybrid Drive Explained
summary: A Blender-animated explanation of the Toyota Hybrid Synergy Drive, showing how the engine, two motor-generators, planetary gearset and battery work together as an eCVT.
why_hn: HN recommends it as the clearest visual explanation of how the Prius power-split hybrid actually works.

title: Deepmind artificial intelligence @ FDOT14
summary: A short smartphone-recorded clip from a 2014 event in Paris where DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis presents an AI learning to play old Atari games. The system learns from only the video signal and the score. Audio quality is poor.
why_hn: HN commenters use it as the canonical demo of deep reinforcement learning, noting that watching it teaches more than an article does.

title: Fun with ultracapacitors!!
summary: Afrotechmods plays with 2600F ultracapacitors that can dump hundreds of amps, shorting them to vaporize bits of metal. Along the way he explains the three most important capacitor equations. The uploader warns that the capacitors are not designed to be shorted.
why_hn: HN commenters use it as a vivid, math-backed demonstration of what ultracapacitors can do and why shorting them is dangerous.

title: Sustainable Energy - Without the Hot Air with David MacKay
summary: David MacKay, scientific advisor to the UK energy department, gives a Harvard talk on sustainable energy at macro and micro scale, drawn from his book Sustainable Energy Without the Hot Air. It stresses the land area renewables require.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an approachable, numbers-driven overview of what renewable energy would take.

title: Robert Sapolsky: The Biology of Humans at Our Best and Worst
summary: A 73-minute Stanford talk by Robert Sapolsky drawn from his book Behave. It surveys the biological factors behind human behavior at its best and worst.
why_hn: HN recommends Sapolsky as an exceptional storyteller and points to this lecture on the biology of human behavior and violence.

title: Steve Jobs' 2005 Stanford Commencement Address (with intro by President John Hennessy)
summary: Steve Jobs' 2005 Stanford commencement address, in which he tells three stories from his life about connecting the dots, love and loss, and death. He urges graduates to follow their dreams and find opportunity in setbacks.
why_hn: HN people point to it as an inspiring, rewatchable speech, especially for anyone worrying about wasted time or direction.

title: Tim Minchin's Storm the Animated Movie
summary: Animated adaptation of Tim Minchin's beat poem 'Storm', in which he argues with a hippie at a London dinner party. It satirizes alternative medicine and defends science and reason.
why_hn: Quoted often for its line on alternative medicine that works being called medicine, and recommended as a full-length listen.

title: Couldn't Care Less. Cormac McCarthy in conversation with David Krakauer
summary: A 2017 documentary filmed at the Santa Fe Institute in which novelist Cormac McCarthy talks with SFI's David Krakauer. They discuss isolation, mathematics, character and the nature of the unconscious.
why_hn: It is one of the few long, candid interviews with the famously reclusive McCarthy, and commenters share it whenever he comes up.

title: Will AI outsmart human intelligence? - with 'Godfather of AI' Geoffrey Hinton
summary: Geoffrey Hinton's 2025 Royal Institution Discourse on what AI has learned from biological intelligence and how it might surpass it. He explains neural networks and argues that human language use resembles what backpropagation-trained networks do.
why_hn: HN readers recommend it as an intuitive explanation of neural networks that shifts how people think about AI and language.

title: How does a Bowling Pinsetter Machine work? (Brunswick GS-X)
summary: Jared Owen's 3D animated breakdown of how a Brunswick GS-X bowling pinsetter works, showing its mechanisms for sweeping, lifting and resetting pins and balls.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an exceptionally well-made explainer of complex mechanical machinery.

title: Ricardo Signes - 闇のEメール伝説
summary: Ricardo Signes' YAPC::Asia Tokyo 2011 talk on the legends and horrors of email: how messy the SMTP and email standards are in practice. The first few minutes are Perl-specific, but the rest applies to anyone handling email.
why_hn: HN points people to it as a funny and sobering warning about why parsing, validating, or implementing email software is far harder than it looks.

title: Bill Hicks - It's Just A Ride
summary: A short clip from Bill Hicks' final special, Revelations, in which he describes life as just a ride. It is a philosophical, calming monologue.
why_hn: Offered as a pick-me-up and calming perspective when people feel lost or stressed.

title: Here's What's Preventing You From Finishing Projects
summary: Zack Freedman gives advice on why makers fail to finish projects, including scrapping bad ideas, showing work publicly and writing a plan that keeps projects fun. It is aimed at hardware DIY but generalizes.
why_hn: HN finds the project-scoping rubric useful for programmers too and recommends it on finishing side projects.

title: Dr Russell Barkley on ADHD Meds and how they all work differently from each other
summary: Dr. Russell Barkley explains how different ADHD medications work and how they differ from one another, in a short clip.
why_hn: HN recommends Barkley as the best resource on ADHD, with clear explanations of what prescription ADHD drugs do.

title: Safe Cycling Showdown - Good vs. Bad City Design - Plus 1 Minus 2
summary: Not Just Bikes compares the same cycling trip to a hardware store in Calgary and in Amsterdam, using a 'plus 1 minus 2' format. It shows how street design shapes how safe and practical cycling is.
why_hn: HN recommends the channel for understanding why North American road design makes cycling dangerous and how the Dutch approach differs.

title: The Time America Almost Stopped Climate Change | Climate Town
summary: Climate Town tells the history of the period when the greenhouse effect was not politically controversial and the US came close to acting on climate. It covers Exxon's early climate science and the policy failures that followed.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an entertaining summary of early bipartisan climate action and corporate influence on research.

title: So... the minute hand shows progression — apparently we think of time in wildly different ways
summary: A Technology Connections video essay on how analog and digital clocks shape different mental models of time, with the minute hand acting as a progress indicator.
why_hn: HN points to it whenever analog versus digital clocks come up, as an idea that changed how commenters think about time perception.

title: The Future of Humanity's Energy No One Knows About | Terraform
summary: A 20-minute S3 episode touring Terraform Industries, a startup making synthetic natural gas from air and solar power. It walks through the reactor, injection system, direct air capture and electrolyzer, plus the company's cost goals and next milestone.
why_hn: HN commenters point to it as a clear, short tour of Terraform's synthetic fuel approach and goals.

title: 13 Misconceptions About Global Warming
summary: Veritasium debunks common climate change myths in under seven minutes, with references to NASA and published research. Topics include CO2 sources, sea ice and 1970s predictions of cooling.
why_hn: Used as a short, well-made rebuttal to common global warming arguments in climate threads.

title: DuckDB – The SQLite for Analytics (Mark Raasveldt, CWI)
summary: Mark Raasveldt of CWI presents DuckDB, an embeddable analytical database described as the SQLite for analytics, in a CMU Database Group talk. He explains why it was built, what it is for, and how it works.
why_hn: HN recommends it as the definitive talk from the implementer on DuckDB's motivation and design.

title: Starlink revisions, Nov 2018
summary: Mark Handley of UCL looks at how SpaceX's November 2018 revisions to the Starlink constellation affect network behavior. The video visualizes the orbits and routing and estimates latencies, building on his earlier video and research paper.
why_hn: HN points to Handley's simulations whenever Starlink latency comes up, as the best visualization of orbits and why laser links could beat fiber over long distances.

title: Obsidian for Beginners: Start HERE — How to Use the Obsidian App for Notes
channel: Linking Your Thinking with Nick Milo
summary: A 12-minute beginner lesson from Nick Milo's Linking Your Thinking series introducing the Obsidian note-taking app and the first steps to start using it.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an approachable start-here demo for people new to Obsidian.

title: Dropping the Bomb: Hiroshima & Nagasaki
summary: A very long video essay by Shaun on the decisions and motivations behind the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, with a detailed timeline and argument that they were not militarily necessary.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a thorough, nuanced account of why the bombings happened and what led Japan to surrender.

title: Simon Sinek: Why Leaders Eat Last
summary: Simon Sinek's 99U talk on why leaders earn trust by putting their team's safety ahead of their own, drawing on biology and anthropology. It distills the ideas of his book Leaders Eat Last into about 46 minutes.
why_hn: HN commenters point to it as a quick way to get the key concepts of the book and as an introduction to leadership thinking.

title: How secure is 256 bit security?
summary: 3Blue1Brown illustrates how enormous the 256-bit search space is, showing how infeasible it is to find a hash or key by guessing and checking.
why_hn: HN uses it as the go-to illustration of just how large 2^256 is.

title: 23. Language
summary: Robert Sapolsky's Stanford lecture on language, comparing human and animal communication, ape language projects like Koko and Kanzi, and how language is acquired. It is part of his human behavioral biology course.
why_hn: HN recommends it, and the whole course, for understanding the brain and language acquisition.

title: 5 steps to designing the life you want  | Bill Burnett | TEDxStanford
summary: TEDxStanford talk by Bill Burnett, executive director of Stanford's design program, on applying design thinking to your own life and career. He offers five practical tips such as getting curious, talking to people and trying things.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a short intro to the Designing Your Life approach when people ask about career direction and finding meaningful work.

title: The Suburbs Are Bleeding America Dry | Climate Town (feat. @NotJustBikes)
summary: A snarky, comedic video essay from Climate Town, with a guest appearance by Not Just Bikes, arguing that American suburban sprawl and single-family zoning are financially and environmentally unsustainable. It covers how zoning rules shape housing and what viewers can do locally, such as attending zoning meetings.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it as an entertaining but well-sourced explainer on US zoning and housing costs whenever those topics come up.

title: How wildlife trade is linked to coronavirus
summary: A Vox explainer on how the wildlife trade and wet markets are linked to coronavirus and why new diseases keep emerging in China. It stresses that most people in China do not eat wildlife.
why_hn: HN commenters shared it during early 2020 as a clear explanation of wet markets and how human encroachment on wildlife drives outbreaks.

title: How to recover from depression
summary: Clinical psychologist Dr Michael Yapko draws on forty years of practice and research to explain skills that help people recover from, and even prevent, depression. He emphasizes cognitive and social factors beyond medication.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a comprehensive talk on depression, and one says it helped them through a bad period.

title: Slavoj Žižek on "They Live" (The Pervert's Guide to Ideology)
summary: A short excerpt from The Pervert's Guide to Ideology in which Slavoj Zizek analyzes John Carpenter's They Live. He uses the film's fight scene and sunglasses to explain how ideology works.
why_hn: HN cites it as a concise, memorable explanation of ideology, often in threads about advertising, propaganda or AI-shaped narratives.

title: The Mental Game of Python - Raymond Hettinger
summary: Raymond Hettinger's PyBay 2019 talk on the mental habits behind effective programming, drawn from coaching, teaching and StackOverflow. He covers problem decomposition, chunking, managing working memory and getting unstuck.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a Python talk with lessons that apply to any programming, especially chunking to manage complexity.

title: Tom Lehrer - New Math (Animated)
summary: An amateur animation of Tom Lehrer's satirical song New Math, which pokes fun at 1960s math teaching and subtraction in base 8. The animation illustrates the old and new subtraction methods.
why_hn: HN brings it up whenever curriculum fads or Common Core complaints appear, as a funny precedent from the 1960s.

title: Celestial Navigation (instruction video)
summary: A roughly 45-minute vintage US military instructional film that gives a comprehensive overview of celestial navigation, covering sextant use and the theory behind lines of position.
why_hn: HN points to it as an unusually clear teaching film on how celestial navigation works, and as an example of how good old military training material is.

title: My stroke of insight | Jill Bolte Taylor | TED
summary: Neuroscientist Jill Bolte Taylor describes watching her own brain functions shut down during a massive stroke. She gives a first-person account of losing speech, motion and self-awareness.
why_hn: Recommended as a vivid first-person view of the right hemisphere in control, often linked to meditation and non-dual experience.

title: Halt and Catch Fire - Sales Call [ "A16" Scene ]
summary: A scene from the TV drama Halt and Catch Fire in which Gordon Clark meets Joe MacMillan, who is posing as an IBM salesman, on a sales call. It includes the dialogue about IBM being the safe choice and a marketing guru telling an engineer when to stop talking.
why_hn: HN commenters post it as a favorite scene about IBM's reputation and sales psychology.

title: Are Space and Time An Illusion?
summary: A PBS Space Time episode hosted by Gabe Perez-Giz on the nature of spacetime and whether space and time are fundamental. It builds up reference frames and causality in a short, dense format.
why_hn: HN commenters point to the PBS Space Time series as a high-quality, bite-sized way to learn modern physics concepts.

title: Michael Levin: Anatomical decision-making by cellular collectives
summary: Michael Levin presents his lab's work on how cellular collectives use bioelectric networks to make anatomical decisions. Topics include pattern memories, regeneration and synthetic living organisms.
why_hn: HN commenters push it as an example of Levin's talks, which they think deserve far more attention.

title: Primitive Technology: Cord drill and Pump drill
summary: Primitive Technology shows building a cord drill from scratch and then upgrading it to a pump drill, using only primitive materials like a stone flywheel and cord.
why_hn: HN people link it as a satisfying demonstration of hand-powered drills being made from nothing.

title: HACKENBUSH: a window to a new world of math
summary: Owen Maitzen's animated hour-long introduction to Hackenbush, a simple combinatorial game, and how its strategy leads to surreal numbers and the roots of the number system.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an accessible, well-visualized entry point to Hackenbush, surreal numbers and their link to Nim.

title: Lee Cronin: Origin of Life, Aliens, Complexity, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #269
primary_topic: origin of life and assembly theory
summary: Lex Fridman interviews University of Glasgow chemist Lee Cronin about the origin of life, aliens, complexity and consciousness. The conversation centers on Cronin's assembly theory.
why_hn: HN points to it in origin-of-life and complexity threads as a fascinating long-form introduction to assembly theory.

title: This is Extremely Dangerous to Our Democracy
summary: A short supercut showing many Sinclair-owned local news anchors reading the same scripted warning about biased news, word for word.
why_hn: HN cites it as a vivid example of coordinated messaging and media consolidation, though some mentions use the title only as a quip.

title: 25c3: The Ultimate Commodore 64 Talk
summary: Michael Steil's 25C3 talk covers the Commodore 64's architecture, quirks and demoscene tricks in about an hour. It aims to convey everything about the machine in a compact, nostalgic tour.
why_hn: HN people treat it as the canonical C64 talk and rewatch Steil's 'Ultimate' series regularly.

title: Sinclair's Soldiers in Trump's War on Media
summary: A Deadspin compilation of local news anchors at Sinclair-owned stations reading the same scripted message about irresponsible one-sided news. It was assembled by Timothy Burke.
why_hn: HN cites it as a vivid example of media consolidation and coordinated messaging.

title: Am I still lactose tolerant? - Lactose Gene Therapy Update
summary: The Thought Emporium's update on the home-brewed gene therapy he took to cure his lactose intolerance. It reports how the effect held up over two years and what future versions might look like.
why_hn: Pointed to as a striking example of DIY biology and self-experimentation with gene therapy.

title: Growing Living Rat Neurons To Play... DOOM? | Part 1
summary: The Thought Emporium grows living rat neurons on an electrode array and tries to train them to play Doom. It is part of a series on biological computing.
why_hn: Cited whenever biocomputing or neurons-on-chip come up, as an accessible example of how such a system can be built.

title: I made a talking banana
summary: A maker builds a talking banana that reads YouTube and Twitch comments aloud on stream, then fights viewers who abuse it with profanity. He ends up building a pronunciation-based filter to catch bad words.
why_hn: HN shares it as a funny, technical story about phonetic profanity filtering, relevant to Soundex and content moderation threads.

title: GDC 2010: Sid Meier Keynote - "Everything You Know is Wrong"
summary: Sid Meier's GDC 2010 keynote on how players perceive probability in games, including how Civilization's odds were adjusted because players misjudged them.
why_hn: HN points to it as the best talk on how people misunderstand probabilities and how designers handle that.

title: 1. A strange determinant
summary: Timothy Gowers thinks aloud, in real time, as he tries to understand why Pascal's determinant equals 1. He does not fully solve it in this episode, but shows his exploratory process.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it to see how a top mathematician approaches an unfamiliar problem through experiments and curiosity.

title: Old car headlights were all the same — which was a fairly bright idea
summary: Technology Connections explains why American cars all had the same standardized sealed-beam headlights until 1957. It covers the regulations behind the design and the effect on night visibility.
why_hn: Recommended as a clear explanation of why old headlights looked as they did, and as a case study in mandating requirements versus solutions.

title: A real person, a lot like you
summary: A three-minute video from Derek Sivers, based on his book Anything You Want, about remembering that the people you deal with online are real people. It contrasts how we treat people face to face with how we treat them online.
why_hn: Recommended in threads about online hostility as a short reminder to treat strangers as human beings.

title: Programming is terrible—Lessons learned from a life wasted. EMF2012
summary: Tef's EMF 2012 talk on lessons from a career in programming, a candid and humorous look at why programming is so often terrible. Slides and a draft script are available online.
why_hn: HN lists it among its favorite programming talks and fantastic technical speeches.

title: RSA ANIMATE: The Divided Brain
summary: An RSA Animate summary of Iain McGilchrist's lecture on the divided brain, arguing the brain's two hemispheres attend to the world differently and that this has shaped culture and society.
why_hn: Recommended as an accessible animated introduction to McGilchrist's thesis on hemispheres and narrow versus diffuse attention.

title: Do we need Attention? - Linear RNNs and State Space Models (SSMs) for NLP
summary: Sasha Rush surveys linear RNNs and state space models as replacements for attention in transformer-style models, in a talk for MLSys. It covers the foundational preliminaries and predates Mamba.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it for building intuition about state space models and the tradeoffs between transformer and SSM layers.

title: 35C3 -  The Ghost in the Machine
summary: Joscha Bach's 35C3 talk offers an AI perspective on the soul, covering perception, mental representation, agency, consciousness and selfhood as things that can arise in a computational system like the brain.
why_hn: HN commenters call it lucid and fluff-free, and point to Bach as one of the most interesting voices on AI, consciousness and philosophy.

title: THIS IS WATER! by David Foster Wallace
summary: A short video of David Foster Wallace's 'This Is Water' commencement speech about awareness and choosing how to think. It argues that the most obvious realities are the hardest to see, using the fish-in-water parable.
why_hn: HN commenters bring it up when urging empathy, patience and attention to the everyday instead of snap judgement.

title: Colonel JD AI Codec Conversation MGS2 HD
summary: The final codec conversation from Metal Gear Solid 2, in which the AI 'Colonel' explains that the Patriots filter out junk information and curate truth for humanity. It plays as a dark meditation on information overload, manipulation and shared reality.
why_hn: Commenters point to it whenever AI-generated content, propaganda or internet garbage comes up, since Kojima seemed to predict it in 2001.

title: Conlang Critic Episode Twelve: Toki Pona
summary: An episode of jan Misali's Conlang Critic series reviewing Toki Pona, a minimalist constructed language with about a hundred words. It is a short, humorous critique of the language's design.
why_hn: Commenters recommend the whole series as an entertaining survey of constructed languages, and this episode when Toki Pona or Lojban comes up.

title: Bret Victor - Drawing Dynamic Visualizations
summary: Bret Victor's talk on Drawing Dynamic Visualizations. It argues that visualization tools offer either the directness of hand drawing or the dynamics of programmed graphics, and shows a tool that combines both.
why_hn: Counted among Bret Victor's best talks and recommended to anyone exploring direct-manipulation tools.

title: How Does SHA-256 Work?
summary: A step-by-step animated explanation of how SHA-256 works, from padding and message schedule to the compression function and final hash, with source code for the animations.
why_hn: Commenters call it clear enough to implement the algorithm from, and teachers use it in courses.

title: [CVPR'21 WAD] Keynote - Andrej Karpathy, Tesla
summary: Andrej Karpathy, then Tesla's head of AI, gives a CVPR 2021 workshop keynote on how Autopilot's neural networks work. A large part covers the move to a vision-only stack, including why radar was dropped and how vision produces depth estimates.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it in Tesla threads as the primary-source explanation of why Tesla removed radar and how its vision depth estimation works.

title: DICKS: Do you need to be one to be a successful leader?
summary: Filmmaker Max Joseph's 35-minute video essay asks whether you have to be a jerk to be a successful leader. It draws on Adam Grant's givers and takers, Robert Greene and famous demanding directors.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a thoughtful critique of the great-leader-as-jerk myth in threads on difficult bosses.

title: Simulating Green Beard Altruism
summary: Primer simulates green beard altruism, where individuals recognize and help others carrying a shared marker, and shows how imposters affect its evolution. It is an animated evolution simulation based on published papers.
why_hn: HN recommends it as part of Primer's strong series of evolution and emergence simulations.

title: The Concept of Language (Noam Chomsky)
summary: Noam Chomsky talks with the University of Washington's Upon Reflection about how languages change over time, why a national language is a modern idea, and how language is a system of communication rooted in human nature.
why_hn: Recommended in threads on language purity and standardization for its clear take that languages are fluid and that national languages are constructed.

title: RSA ANIMATE: First as Tragedy, Then as Farce
summary: An RSA Animate adaptation of a Slavoj Zizek talk on charitable giving and ethical consumerism. It argues that buying products that bundle a charity donation can sustain the system that causes the problems.
why_hn: Frequently linked in threads on philanthropy, ethical consumption and billionaire giving as a short, approachable critique of charity.

title: Do schools kill creativity? | Sir Ken Robinson | TED
summary: Sir Ken Robinson argues, with humor and stories such as that of choreographer Gillian Lynne, that education systems undermine creativity and should be changed. It is one of the most viewed TED talks.
why_hn: HN refers to it constantly in schooling debates, as a favorite talk or as the basis for arguments about creativity, though some commenters dispute its conclusions.

title: Who Is Responsible For Climate Change? – Who Needs To Fix It?
summary: Kurzgesagt examines who is responsible for climate change, comparing historical, current and per-capita emissions by country. It argues that individual footprints are a distraction from larger responsibility.
why_hn: Recommended as a nuanced, data-backed treatment of emissions responsibility, made with Our World in Data.

title: The Ultimate AeroPress Technique (Episode #3)
summary: James Hoffmann demonstrates his AeroPress technique with a short recipe: 11g of coffee, 200g of just-boiled water, a 2-minute immersion, then a press. He explains why he skips rinsing, preheating and inverting.
why_hn: HN coffee fans cite it as a forgiving, repeatable recipe that gives good results.

title: The "Last Lecture" by Randy Pausch
summary: Randy Pausch, a Carnegie Mellon computer scientist and virtual reality pioneer who was dying of cancer, gives his 'Last Lecture' about achieving childhood dreams and living well. The recording is a full-length talk of about 104 minutes.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as an emotionally powerful life-advice talk and revisit it as a reminder of mortality.

title: Gambling and the desire machine | Pay to Win
summary: A 70-minute video essay by Jimmy McGee on gambling, addiction and game design, tracing horse racing, slot machines and collectible card markets. It is the first in a series on making money from games.
why_hn: Recommended as an engaging, well-researched look at the history of gambling machines and how games borrow their psychology.

title: 2017 Personality 01: Introduction
summary: The opening lecture of Jordan Peterson's 2017 University of Toronto personality course. He defines personality from historical, constructivist, psychoanalytic, behavioral and neuropsychological angles.
why_hn: Recommended as part of a long lecture series on psychology, complementing biology lectures, and named when HN asks for the best lecture series.

title: BOOKSTORES: How to Read More Books in the Golden Age of Content
summary: A short film by Max Joseph about his anxiety in bookstores and how to read more books amid constant streaming, social media and news. He looks for ways to rebalance his content diet in favor of reading.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it as a thoughtful mini-doc on reading time and frequency in the age of social media.

title: Euler's formula with introductory group theory
summary: 3Blue1Brown builds intuition for Euler's formula, e^(pi i) = -1, using the core ideas of group theory. It treats exponentiation geometrically as rotation and scaling instead of repeated multiplication.
why_hn: Recommended as a mind-opening, visual explanation of why Euler's formula is true.

title: Loneliness
summary: Kurzgesagt explains why humans feel loneliness, its evolutionary role, and how modern life can turn it into a harmful downward spiral. It cites research and offers ideas on what to do about it.
why_hn: Shared in loneliness threads as a well-sourced, empathetic explanation, including for people struggling with it.

title: The Power of Big Data and Psychographics | 2016 Concordia Annual Summit
summary: Alexander Nix of Cambridge Analytica presents at the 2016 Concordia Summit on using big data, psychographic profiling and behavioral microtargeting in elections.
why_hn: HN points to it as the company's own pitch, used in debates about data-driven manipulation and extrapolated to today's AI.

title: Do we see reality as it is? | Donald Hoffman | TED
summary: Cognitive scientist Donald Hoffman argues in this TED talk that evolution shaped perception to track fitness rather than truth. He uses evolutionary simulations and the Australian jewel beetle as examples.
why_hn: Cited in discussions of perception, consciousness and what is real, though some commenters find his conclusions hand-wavy.

title: Fast Inverse Square Root — A Quake III Algorithm
summary: A walkthrough of the Quake III fast inverse square root, explaining where the constant 0x5f3759df comes from. It covers IEEE 754 floats, the bit hack that approximates a logarithm, and a Newton's method refinement.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an approachable explanation that makes the famous algorithm finally make sense.

title: Efficient Bayesian inference with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo -- Michael Betancourt (Part 1)
summary: Michael Betancourt's lecture at MLSS Iceland 2014 on efficient Bayesian inference with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. It covers MCMC concepts and motivation and the problems of sampling in high-dimensional distributions.
why_hn: HN people return to it as a clear primer on MCMC and HMC and on why high dimensions behave counterintuitively.

title: Daniel Suarez: The kill decision shouldn't belong to a robot
summary: Novelist Daniel Suarez warns in a TED talk about autonomous robotic weapons and drones. He argues that taking the decision to kill out of human hands threatens democratic accountability and calls for a ban.
why_hn: Plugged repeatedly in AI and drone threads as a concise statement of the dangers of automated weapons.

title: The NCAA: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
summary: John Oliver's Last Week Tonight segment on the NCAA, arguing that the organization profits enormously from college athletes while insisting they remain unpaid amateurs. It covers the money in college sports, including big-school athletic spending, and the case for paying athletes.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it as a sharp, accessible primer on the NCAA's amateurism model and athlete compensation, including for readers outside the US.

title: University of Texas at Austin 2014 Commencement Address - Admiral William H. McRaven
summary: Admiral William McRaven's 2014 University of Texas commencement address, built around lessons from Navy SEAL training. It famously opens with the case for making your bed every morning.
why_hn: Recommended in life-advice and motivation threads as worth watching in full, especially for its point about starting small by changing yourself.

title: C++ Seasoning
hn_categories: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
summary: Sean Parent's GoingNative 2013 talk surveys new and overlooked C++ features and shows how to use them for simple, correct, clear code. It stresses using standard algorithms rather than raw loops.
why_hn: Recommended whenever the STL mindset or avoiding raw loops in C++ comes up, as an enlightening talk on expressive algorithms.

title: The User is Drunk
summary: A short talk by Will Dayble of Squareweave arguing that you should design software as if the user were drunk: distracted, impaired in attention and vision, and prone to misreading. It is a user experience talk built around that framing.
why_hn: HN users recommend it as a memorable, short way to build empathy for users' confusing mistakes and to design for distraction.

title: How I animate 3Blue1Brown | A Manim demo with Ben Sparks
summary: Grant Sanderson of 3Blue1Brown shows his workflow for animating math videos with Manim, with Ben Sparks. He codes scenes live, including a Lorenz attractor, and walks through example scenes.
why_hn: Recommended as a rare detailed look at how 3b1b videos are made, including live debugging of his rendering engine.

title: The puzzle of motivation | Dan Pink | TED
summary: Dan Pink's TED talk argues that traditional carrot-and-stick rewards often fail for creative work, drawing on the candle problem and social science research. He points to autonomy, mastery and purpose as better motivators.
why_hn: HN cites it whenever money as an incentive comes up, as evidence that rewards can backfire for creative white-collar work.

title: How To Draw Mushrooms On An Oscilloscope With Sound
summary: Jerobeam Fenderson shows how to draw a mushroom on an oscilloscope in XY mode using stereo audio, then animates it by modulating with a larger wave. Pd and Max4Live patches are provided.
why_hn: HN finds it mesmerizing and uses it to build intuition for waveforms and oscilloscope XY drawing.

title: Is Nuclear Waste Really Waste?
summary: In a 2010 Google Tech Talk, Kirk Sorensen gives an economic analysis of what spent nuclear fuel actually contains. He argues it is mostly valuable material that can be partitioned and reused, not just waste to be isolated for 100,000 years.
why_hn: HN readers recommend it as the best explanation of what nuclear waste really is and how much of it is reusable fuel.

title: Jancovici : Will technology save us from Climate Change ? MIT Media Lab - 23/02/2021
summary: Jean-Marc Jancovici gives an MIT Media Lab talk on whether technology can save us from climate change. He argues from a physical view of energy that economic growth, energy use and climate impact are tightly linked.
why_hn: Recommended in climate and energy threads as a numbers-based explanation of why energy underlies growth and emissions.

title: Making a Full Bridge Rectifier
summary: ElectroBOOM's Mehdi Sadaghdar explains how a full bridge rectifier works, the building block of AC to DC converters, with his usual humor and a demonstration of the circuit.
why_hn: Recommended as an enlightening and funny explanation of bridge rectifiers, often linked in power supply teardown threads.

title: The Neuroanatomy of ADHD and thus how to treat ADHD - CADDAC - Dr Russel Barkley part 3ALL
summary: Dr. Russell Barkley lectures on the neuroanatomy of ADHD and how to treat it, linking executive function and working memory to the disorder. It is part 3 of a CADDAC series.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it to people with ADHD for helping them understand their behavior and how their brain works.

title: The Ultimate French Press Technique
summary: James Hoffmann demonstrates his technique for a clean, sludge-free cup from a French press: stir, break the crust, wait, and carefully pour. It is a four-minute guide.
why_hn: HN commenters swear by it as the best way to make French press coffee, and cite its 16:1 water-to-coffee ratio.

title: RSA ANIMATE: Smile or Die
summary: An RSA Animate drawing of Barbara Ehrenreich's talk on the darker side of positive thinking. It argues that forced positivity in culture, work and policy can be harmful and played a part in the financial crisis.
why_hn: HN uses it as a go-to short critique of mandatory positivity in workplaces, startups and corporate culture.

title: Hamming, "n-Dimensional Space" (April 14, 1995)
summary: Richard Hamming's 1995 lecture on n-dimensional space, showing how geometric intuition about spheres and cubes breaks down in high dimensions. It is part of his course on learning to learn.
why_hn: Recommended as the source for counterintuitive high-dimensional geometry and described as an eye opener.

title: selective attention test
summary: The original invisible gorilla awareness test by Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris, in which viewers count basketball passes and often miss a gorilla crossing the scene. It demonstrates inattentional blindness.
why_hn: HN uses it constantly as the classic demonstration that attention is selective, in threads on driving, motorcycles, AI and perception.

title: Charlie Rose: Sir James Goldsmith Interview - 15.11.94
summary: Charlie Rose interviews Sir James Goldsmith in 1994 about the coming GATT free-trade agreement. Goldsmith predicts that global capital mobility will upset the balance between capital and labor.
why_hn: Recommended as a prescient interview on free trade and its social consequences, worth watching with hindsight.

title: Errol Morris interviews mob lawyer Murray Richman - 1/3
summary: Part one of Errol Morris's First Person interview with Murray Richman, a New York lawyer who defends mob figures. He talks about how he sees the law and his clients.
why_hn: HN recommends it as the best interview of Morris's series and as an insight into how the law and ordinary people's minds work.

title: Let’s go whaling: Tricks for monetising mobile game players with free-to-play
summary: A 2016 conference talk by a mobile game CEO on the tricks of free-to-play monetization, including player profiles and how to target high-spending whales.
why_hn: HN mostly cites it critically, as an insider's blunt playbook for psychologically exploiting players in F2P and loot box games.

title: Alec Baldwin - Best performance
summary: The famous Alec Baldwin monologue from the film Glengarry Glen Ross, where his character Blake berates salesmen with the 'Always Be Closing' speech. It is a short, profane scene about sales pressure and motivation.
why_hn: HN points to it as the one scene worth watching from the movie, a classic about sales and entrepreneurship.

title: Ryan Dahl: Original Node.js presentation
summary: Ryan Dahl's first presentation of Node.js at JSConf 2009. He pitches event-driven, non-blocking I/O as the motivation, rather than JavaScript itself.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a classic dev tool pitch with palpable energy, and cites it for why Node was created.

title: Sulforaphane and Its Effects on Cancer, Mortality, Aging, Brain and Behavior, Heart Disease & More
summary: Rhonda Patrick of FoundMyFitness makes a case for isothiocyanates such as sulforaphane from cruciferous vegetables and broccoli sprouts. It covers cancer, aging, heart disease, brain and behavior, and neurodegeneration, with chapter timestamps.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a science-backed overview of sulforaphane's health effects, particularly for cancer.

title: Google Developers Day US - Python Design Patterns
summary: Alex Martelli's Google Developers Day talk on classic design patterns (creational, structural and behavioral) and how they appear in Python. He stresses that patterns must be studied in the context of the implementing language.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a level-headed, practical take on design patterns without Java-style verbosity.

title: Brené Brown on Empathy
summary: A short animated RSA piece with Dr Brene Brown's voiceover on the difference between empathy and sympathy. She argues that real connection requires getting in touch with your own vulnerability, rather than trying to fix someone's pain.
why_hn: Recommended as a quick, memorable explanation of how to support someone in pain without making it about yourself.

title: Why It's Impossible to Tune a Piano
summary: A minutephysics video explaining why a piano cannot be perfectly tuned, comparing equal temperament with just intonation and the math of harmonics.
why_hn: Commenters link it as a quick, clear explanation of why twelve notes only approximate simple ratios.

title: The Trolley Problem in Real Life
summary: Vsauce's Michael Stevens stages a realistic version of the trolley problem with unsuspecting subjects who believe they must decide a life-or-death outcome. The Mind Field episode compares what people say they would do with what they actually do.
why_hn: Recommended as a worthwhile real-world experiment whenever trolley problems or moral dilemmas come up.

title: Permaculture Greening the Desert - Geoff Lawton
summary: Geoff Lawton documents a permaculture project that turned barren Jordanian desert into green, productive land. It covers the techniques he used.
why_hn: Cited in climate and carbon-removal threads as an inspiring example of re-greening deserts.

title: "The Clean Code Talks  -- Inheritance, Polymorphism, & Testing"
summary: Misko Hevery's Clean Code Talk shows how to use object-oriented techniques such as polymorphism to remove repeated if and switch statements. The result is code that is easier to test, understand and maintain.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a thorough treatment of replacing conditionals with polymorphism and why flags and deep ifs can be code smells.

title: SHIPBREAKERS | Would you risk your life dismantling the world’s largest ships just to survive? | NFB
summary: An NFB documentary about the shipbreaking yards of Alang, India, where about 40,000 people dismantle huge ships by hand in dangerous conditions.
why_hn: HN recommends it for an up-close look at the shipbreaking industry.

title: Which key is the saddest?
summary: Musician Adam Neely examines whether certain keys sound sadder than others, looking at the history of tuning systems and temperaments and at how instrument timbre shapes the emotional character we hear. It draws on historical aesthetics writing and audio examples.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it for its historical context on tuning systems and for how instruments influence what music gets composed.

title: Carbon Offsets: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
summary: A Last Week Tonight segment explaining carbon offsets, what they claim to do, and how they may worsen climate change. It looks at perverse incentives and questionable projects.
why_hn: HN points to it as an informative explainer on why many carbon offset schemes are not genuine.

title: Laws that choke creativity | Larry Lessig
summary: Larry Lessig's TED talk argues that copyright law chokes creativity, drawing on John Philip Sousa, celestial copyrights and the ASCAP cartel to make the case for reviving remix culture.
why_hn: Recommended in copyright, patent and SOPA threads as a clear case for copyright reform.

title: Meaningful Play: Getting Gamification Right
summary: A Google Tech Talk by Sebastian Deterding on gamification. It looks at what points and badges get wrong and what lessons game design offers for non-game applications.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a thoughtful take on doing gamification and game design well.

title: Craig Ferguson Speaks From The Heart
summary: A clip of Craig Ferguson's late-night monologue in which he talks about his past as an alcoholic. He explains why he will not mock Britney Spears over her breakdown.
why_hn: HN users share it in threads on drinking and addiction as an honest account of alcoholism and sobriety.

title: The Secret Chinese War for Your Opinion!
summary: Serpentza, a Westerner living in China, describes Chinese influence efforts abroad and the cultural conflict between Shen Yun and Confucius Institutes. It is a commentary from his personal perspective.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as an interesting on-the-ground perspective on Confucius Institutes and Chinese influence operations.

title: My Gift To Climate Alarmists
summary: Tony Heller presents a short video arguing that climate science relies on data truncation, cherry-picking and selective presentation of statistics. It is a one-sided polemic against mainstream climate claims.
why_hn: Shared by climate-skeptic commenters as a counter-argument to alarmist statistics, a contested source rather than consensus.

title: Johnny Cash - Hurt
summary: The official music video for Johnny Cash's cover of Nine Inch Nails' Hurt, from his American Recordings era, filmed late in his life. It is a stark, emotional performance of the song.
why_hn: HN commenters hold it up as one of the greatest cover versions ever, so powerful that Trent Reznor said the song was no longer his.

title: The Long, Twisted And Slightly Ridiculous Story of Avgas Part 1
summary: AVweb's Paul Bertorelli explains why general aviation has failed to replace leaded avgas, blaming industry inertia, bureaucratic delay and an exemption that removes the incentive. This is part one of two.
why_hn: HN recommends the series as an insightful, humorous account of why unleaded aviation fuel is so hard to approve.

title: How did consciousness evolve? - with Nicholas Humphrey
summary: A Royal Institution lecture in which Nicholas Humphrey presents his theory of phenomenal consciousness and its evolution. He draws on the book Sentience and discusses evidence for animal sentience.
why_hn: Recommended as a good high-level view of Humphrey's book and his argument on how consciousness evolved.

title: #NSDR (Non-Sleep Deep Rest) with Dr. Andrew Huberman
summary: A roughly 10-minute guided Non-Sleep Deep Rest session voiced by neuroscientist Andrew Huberman. It is meant to reduce daytime fatigue, improve focus and aid sleep.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a short, practical guided rest session to use during a midday break or nap.

title: Forget big change, start with a tiny habit: BJ Fogg at TEDxFremont
summary: BJ Fogg of Stanford's Persuasive Tech Lab argues that lasting change comes from tiny habits, such as flossing one tooth or doing one pushup, anchored to things you already do.
why_hn: Recommended in habit and motivation threads for its simple anchor-then-tiny-action recipe.

title: Chess Fundamentals #1: Undefended Pieces
summary: First video in John Bartholomew's Chess Fundamentals series, focused on spotting undefended pieces. He teaches habits for scanning your own and your opponent's position to avoid hanging pieces.
why_hn: HN chess improvers recommend Bartholomew's beginner playlist as a clear, approachable path to getting better.

title: Freeman Dyson on the Global Warming Hysteria April, 2015
summary: A 2015 interview in which physicist Freeman Dyson, then 91, argues that global warming concerns are exaggerated, that CO2 is beneficial and that climate models oversimplify complex systems. It is posted on a channel that opposes climate consensus.
why_hn: HN commenters point to it as a prominent physicist's skeptical counter-view, usually when someone asks for dissenting opinions.

title: Veritasium: A Story of YouTube Propaganda
summary: Tom Nicholas critiques Veritasium's sponsored video on driverless cars, using it to examine YouTube sponsorships, science-channel credibility and how statistics and misinformation can be used in branded content.
why_hn: HN cites it in discussions of sponsored science content and Veritasium's credibility, usually as the go-to critique.

title: Infinite fractions and the most irrational number
summary: Mathologer uses continued fractions to show why the golden ratio is the most irrational number, comparing it with root 2, e and pi and pointing to where this shows up in nature.
why_hn: Recommended as a clear, visual explanation of continued fractions and why phi is hardest to approximate by fractions.

title: I Have Delivered Value... But At What Cost?
summary: A short KRAZAM comedy sketch satirizing corporate tech life, where a worker reckons with having delivered value at the cost of his soul, complete with Slack chimes.
why_hn: Praised as painfully accurate office satire, with the channel's sketches called genius.

title: The Fallen of World War II
summary: Neil Halloran's animated, data-driven documentary visualizes the human cost of World War II and compares it with other wars and the trend toward fewer war deaths in recent decades.
why_hn: HN cites it for a sense of the scale of WWII casualties by country and the long decline in violence.

title: Bret Victor - Inventing on Principle
summary: Bret Victor's talk from Dropbox's DBX conference about living by a guiding principle, in his case that creators need an immediate connection to what they are making. He shows live-coding and time-manipulation demos that let ideas take form at the speed of thought.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it as the best demonstration of why instant feedback matters in programming tools.

title: Making Badass Developers - Kathy Sierra (Serious Pony) keynote
summary: Kathy Sierra's Fluent 2015 keynote on the one metaskill for developers: the ability to come up to speed quickly and stay there. She covers how people learn, cognitive resources versus willpower, and building skill.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it when asked how to learn better or keep improving.

title: America's Nerve Gas Arsenal
summary: A 1973 NBC News documentary on the US nerve gas arsenal, covering leaks in Okinawa, a Utah test that killed thousands of sheep, and the long-term hazards of storage sites. It won an Emmy.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a fascinating, Emmy-winning look at US chemical weapons stockpiles and their dangers.

title: Jim Keller: The Future of Computing, AI, Life, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #162
summary: Lex Fridman interviews chip architect Jim Keller about the future of computing, AI, life and consciousness. Topics include CPU design, branch prediction and why imperfect designs often win.
why_hn: Recommended as a stellar long-form interview with someone both very smart and wise, mined for CPU design insights.

title: RAAIS 2017 - Simon Knowles, Co-Founder and CTO of Graphcore
channel: The Research and Applied AI Summit - RAAIS
summary: Simon Knowles, co-founder and CTO of Graphcore, talks about "intelligence processors", chips designed specifically for machine learning. The talk was given at the RAAIS 2017 summit and covers Graphcore's architecture.
why_hn: HN points to it as a technical talk from a chip designer on why AI hardware should put memory close to compute and use async data transfers.

title: The call to learn | Clifford Stoll
summary: Clifford Stoll's energetic TED talk, a wandering mix of anecdotes, a science experiment and thoughts on curiosity, education and technology. He is the author of The Cuckoo's Egg.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it for Stoll's infectious enthusiasm and his case for teaching kids science, and often mention it in threads about him and his Klein bottles.

title: Noam Chomsky on Propaganda - The Big Idea - Interview with Andrew Marr
summary: A 1996 BBC interview in which Noam Chomsky explains his propaganda model of the media to Andrew Marr, including how filters shape what journalists report and the role of self-censorship.
why_hn: Recommended and quoted in threads on media bias, press and power, and self-censorship.

title: How to Get Good at Small Talk, and Even Enjoy It
summary: A Harvard Business Review video with tactics for getting better at small talk and enjoying it, such as setting goals, allowing pauses, and starting and ending conversations.
why_hn: HN commenters share it as a short, practical resource for people who struggle with small talk.

title: Classic Game Postmortem - Another World
summary: Eric Chahi's GDC 2011 postmortem of Another World (Out of This World), describing how he built the game. He shows his polygon art approach, rotoscoping and animation tools.
why_hn: HN points to it whenever Another World comes up, as one of the better GDC talks by the game's creator.

title: Denmark's Forest Kindergartens
summary: An SBS Dateline short documentary on Danish forest kindergartens, where children play freely outdoors, climb trees and use knives with little adult intervention.
why_hn: Recommended as a concise look at the culture behind outdoor kindergartens in threads on parenting and education.

title: DEFCON 19: Steal Everything, Kill Everyone, Cause Total Financial Ruin! (w speaker)
summary: Jayson E. Street's DEF CON 19 talk shows photos from real security engagements where he was already inside client facilities, illustrating how social engineering and physical intrusion can cause huge losses. For each attack he also explains what defenses would have stopped him.
why_hn: It is a repeat pick in 'favorite tech talk' threads as a funny, eye-opening look at how easily physical security and people can be bypassed.

title: Former fusion scientist on why we won't have fusion power by 2040
summary: A former fusion scientist argues why fusion power by 2040 is unrealistic, covering the physics challenges, neutron issues and optimistic company claims, with a brief note of good news.
why_hn: Praised as the best crash course on fusion reactor design nuances from an insider, used to temper fusion hype.

title: The Secret Life of Machines - Vacuum Cleaners  1/2
summary: Part 1 of an episode of the British educational TV series The Secret Life of Machines, about how vacuum cleaners work and their history. It mixes humor with explanation of household technology.
why_hn: HN recommends the series as an entertaining way to learn how everyday machines work, enough to start debugging them.

title: Computers for Cynics 0 - The Myth of Technology
summary: The opening episode of Ted Nelson's Computers for Cynics series, in which he casts doubt on conventional accounts of computer basics. He argues that conventions and packaging are mistaken for technology.
why_hn: HN likes it for Nelson's habit of reframing computing history so that past decisions look arbitrary.

title: Salad Mug - DYNAMO DREAM, Ep1
summary: The first episode of Ian Hubert's Dynamo Dream series, a one-person sci-fi short made in Blender with a gritty futuristic city setting. It was made with help from friends and Patreon supporters over about three years.
why_hn: HN holds it up as an impressive example of what a tiny team can achieve with Blender.

title: "Liberating the Smalltalk lurking in C and Unix" by Stephen Kell
primary_topic: dynamic features in c and unix
hn_categories: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
summary: Stephen Kell's Strange Loop talk argues that C and Unix already contain Smalltalk-like dynamism and introspection that can be exposed. He presents his liballocs research on bridging dynamic and compiled languages.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it in Smalltalk and Unix threads as a demonstration of runtime dynamism hiding in native binaries and shared libraries.

title: JSON Parser 100% From Scratch in Haskell (only 111 lines)
summary: Tsoding live-codes a JSON parser from scratch in Haskell in about 111 lines, using only the standard library. It is an edited Twitch stream that explains the intuition behind parser combinators, functors, applicatives and monads.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a hands-on way to understand Haskell and parser combinators by watching a parser get built live.

title: The psychology of evil | Philip Zimbardo
summary: Psychologist Philip Zimbardo explains how ordinary people can be pushed into doing evil by situations and systems. He draws on the Stanford prison experiment and unseen Abu Ghraib photos, then turns to the opposite case: how ordinary people can become heroes.
why_hn: HN uses it to argue that systems rather than bad apples drive cruelty, and for its section on how anonymity changes behavior.

title: CS480/680 Lecture 19: Attention and Transformer Networks
summary: A university lecture from CS480/680 by Pascal Poupart on attention mechanisms and transformer networks, worked through on a chalkboard.
why_hn: HN recommends it to newcomers as a clear explanation of attention, including the query/key/value intuition.

title: The complete FUN TO IMAGINE with Richard Feynman
summary: All six episodes of the 1983 BBC series Fun to Imagine, in which Richard Feynman muses on jiggling atoms, fire, rubber bands, magnets, electricity and more. He explains how to think about nature and why imagination is fun.
why_hn: HN recommends it for Feynman's intuitive explanations and his joy in understanding how things work.

title: Ira Glass on the Creative Process (www.getoutthebox.org)
summary: A two-minute video of Ira Glass on the creative process, describing the gap between taste and skill when starting out and urging you to keep producing until your work matches your taste.
why_hn: Shared as encouragement for beginners learning design or craft, on persisting through the taste-skill gap.

title: Charlie Brooker's Newswipe 25/03/09
summary: A clip from Charlie Brooker's Newswipe in which a forensic psychiatrist argues that intense news coverage of school shooters encourages copycat attacks, alongside Brooker's satire of formulaic news reporting.
why_hn: HN cites it in discussions about how media should report mass shootings, as an expert-backed argument for not glorifying perpetrators.

title: Daniel Henry Holmes Ingalls Jr.: The Live Web. Drag 'n drop in the cloud
summary: Smalltalk pioneer Dan Ingalls presents the Lively Kernel at JSConf US 2012, a live, direct-manipulation programming environment running in the browser. He shows drag-and-drop building of live objects on the web.
why_hn: Commenters link it as a demo of what a live, inspectable, Smalltalk-style environment in the browser can be, in threads about Alan Kay, Smalltalk and web limitations.

title: #NoEstimates (Allen Holub)
summary: Allen Holub's keynote arguing that estimation is harmful, particularly in Agile, and presenting planning approaches based on data and flow instead. It covers the distinction between estimation and data-driven prediction.
why_hn: Recommended in estimation and sprint debates as a well-reasoned account of where waste is and isn't in agile.

title: The ascent of Alex Honnold
summary: A CBS News (60 Minutes) profile of free solo climber Alex Honnold, who scales sheer rock faces without ropes. Lara Logan reports on his climbing and his apparent lack of fear, including his Half Dome ascent.
why_hn: HN commenters point to it as a nerve-wracking look at Honnold's free soloing, often when climbing, risk or van life comes up.

title: Why this British crossroads was so dangerous
summary: Tom Scott explains why Ipley Cross in England's New Forest was one of Britain's most dangerous junctions. The angled crossroads lets a car's A-pillar hide approaching traffic and cyclists because there is no relative motion in the driver's view.
why_hn: Used as the go-to visual demonstration of A-pillar blind spots and badly designed junctions.

title: How to Achieve Your Most Ambitious Goals | Stephen Duneier | TEDxTucson
summary: Stephen Duneier describes a decision-making approach that took him from struggling with simple tasks to achieving ambitious goals. The talk centers on breaking goals into small marginal adjustments.
why_hn: HN people recommend it for its simple, powerful idea of marginal adjustments and its usefulness for tackling big projects.

title: Arcologies
summary: An Isaac Arthur episode on arcologies, self-sufficient habitats that could house whole cities, on Earth or on harsh worlds. It covers how such structures might work and what limits their size.
why_hn: HN commenters point to it in population and megacity discussions, mainly for its estimates of how many people arcologies could support and the heat, power and elevator bottlenecks.

title: Ricky Jay - Amazing Card Trick/Manipulation
summary: A three-minute clip of magician Ricky Jay performing a card manipulation routine, including table faro shuffles. The routine builds in intensity and ends with a surprising finish.
why_hn: HN people share it as a classic example of sleight-of-hand mastery whose ending is mind-blowing.

title: You Suck at Photoshop - Distort, Warp, & Layer Effects
summary: An episode of the comedic You Suck at Photoshop series in which Donnie Hoyle teaches distort, warp and layer effects while vandalizing a Vanagon in the image. It won Webby awards as a how-to and comedy series.
why_hn: Recommended as a classic, funny Photoshop tutorial series with a strong comedic personality.

title: Joe Armstrong & Jeremy Ruston - Intertwingling the Tiddlywiki with Erlang | Code Mesh LDN 18
summary: Joe Armstrong, creator of Erlang, and Jeremy Ruston, creator of TiddlyWiki, discuss hypertext, Ted Nelson's idea of intertwingled knowledge, and a way to combine TiddlyWiki with Erlang. It is a Code Mesh LDN 2018 talk.
why_hn: Recommended in note-taking and personal wiki threads for its enthusiasm about granular, densely linked notes and TiddlyWiki.

title: Growing Human Neurons on a Home Made Electrode Array
summary: The Thought Emporium builds a homemade multi-electrode array, grows human neurons on it and attempts to take readings. It is the first part of a series aimed at connecting living neurons to a computer.
why_hn: HN cites it as an impressive garage-science example of neuron-computer interfaces and hard-science DIY biology.

title: Principles of economics, translated
summary: Economist-comedian Yoram Bauman delivers a humorous translation of Mankiw's ten principles of economics for the uninitiated. It was presented at the AAAS humor session in 2007.
why_hn: HN points to it as a short, funny and genuinely informative take on economic principles such as trade and opportunity cost.

title: Everything is a Remix (2023 Edition)
summary: Kirby Ferguson's updated four-part video essay arguing that creativity is built on copying, transforming and combining existing work. It covers examples from film, music and technology and touches on generative AI.
why_hn: Pointed to in copyright and AI debates as a compelling case that all culture is remix.

title: Who’s Taking America’s Water? | Climate Town
summary: A Climate Town episode on who uses America's water, particularly Western water. It looks at agriculture such as alfalfa and animal feed, and at water-rights rules that discourage conservation.
why_hn: HN points to it in Colorado River and water-use threads as an accessible explainer of why the Western water shortage keeps getting worse.

title: How the US Postal Service reads terrible handwriting
summary: Tom Scott visits the USPS Remote Encoding Center in Salt Lake City, where keyers decipher mail images machines cannot read. It shows the lengths taken to decode bad handwriting.
why_hn: Recommended in address and OCR threads as a look at the last human mail-coding operation.

title: Badness 0 (Apostrophe‛s version)
summary: Tom 7's pilot episode of a series that plays with type systems and absurd programming, presented as a parody of the GPL v3 license. It mixes a typesetting experiment with a long, story-driven intro on the origin of TeX. Source code and papers are linked from the author's site.
why_hn: HN readers point to it as an example of Tom7's ridiculous-but-brilliant programming projects, here tied to license parody and typesetting.

title: I Solved Klotski
summary: 2swap explains how he solved the Klotski sliding-block puzzle by mapping its full state space as a graph and visualizing it. The video includes footage of the Guinness world-record solve and links to an interactive graph.
why_hn: HN people point to it for intuition about why some games are hard to navigate and for its Rush Hour and graph visualizations.

title: Solaris | SCIENCE FICTION | FULL MOVIE | directed by Tarkovsky
summary: Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 film Solaris, in which a psychologist is sent to a space station orbiting a planet with an alien intelligence and meets his dead wife there. It is the full movie, uploaded by Mosfilm.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a masterpiece of emotional, contemplative science fiction, and draws analogies between its alien ocean and AI.

title: Navy pilots describe encounters with UFOs
summary: A 60 Minutes segment in which Navy pilots describe encounters with unidentified aerial phenomena, ahead of a report due to Congress.
why_hn: HN commenters point to it as eyewitness testimony and multi-radar evidence in UFO threads, though some dispute it.

title: Thank You For Your Feedback - Don't Say Velcro
summary: Velcro's follow-up to its "Don't Say Velcro" ad responds to viewer feedback, with a humorous take on trademark usage and alternative names for hook and loop fasteners.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a delightful sequel to the original ad, brought up in threads on trademarks and the original campaign.

title: 50 Years Ago, This Was a Wasteland. He Changed Everything | Short Film Showcase
summary: An 8-minute National Geographic short film about David Bamberger, who bought 5,500 overgrazed acres in the Texas Hill Country and restored the land and its aquifers over about 50 years.
why_hn: Cited in climate and water threads as an encouraging example of large-scale landscape restoration.

title: Causal understanding of water displacement by a crow
summary: A silent PLOS ONE video of New Caledonian crows solving Aesop's Fable puzzles by dropping objects to raise water and reach food. It shows example trials from experiments testing causal understanding of water displacement.
why_hn: Used as vivid evidence of crow intelligence and animal physical reasoning in discussions of cognition.

title: The Hustle
summary: A KRAZAM satirical sketch about hustle culture and productivity obsession in tech.
why_hn: HN posts it as a joke in productivity and focus threads, and some praise the channel as pitch-perfect satire of tech stereotypes.

title: The Insane Engineering of James Webb Telescope
summary: Real Engineering explains the engineering behind the James Webb Space Telescope, including its folding mirror, sunshield, orbit and cooling systems, and why deployment was so difficult.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an accessible in-depth explanation of how Webb works and why its deployment was remarkable.

title: Why Life Seems to Speed Up as We Age
summary: Veritasium explores why time seems to speed up as we age, covering chronoception and several competing explanations beyond the common proportional-theory argument.
why_hn: Cited in threads about perceived time as a good, detailed explanation of the effect.

title: Pentagon Wars - Bradley Fighting Vehicle Evolution
summary: A roughly ten-minute scene from the movie The Pentagon Wars showing how the Bradley Fighting Vehicle's requirements ballooned through committee demands into a compromised design. It is a satirical dramatization of military procurement.
why_hn: Linked in nearly every F-35 or procurement thread as the classic illustration of feature creep and design by stakeholder committee, including in software.

title: Why We Sleep: Science of Sleep & Dreams | Matthew Walker | Talks at Google
summary: Berkeley sleep scientist Matthew Walker presents the science of sleep and dreams and how sleep affects health and lifespan, based on his book Why We Sleep.
why_hn: HN suggests it as an easy alternative to the book for people who want Walker's sleep findings.

title: Why Starting A Rocket Engine Is So Hard!
summary: Tim Dodd's hour-long deep dive on how rocket engines start, from solid motors to liquid engines. It covers thermal conditioning, spin-up, ignition methods, starting in space, and a step-by-step RS-25 startup.
why_hn: HN recommends it as the best explanation of why engine start is hard and what can go wrong.

title: Why CG Sucks (Except It Doesn't)
summary: RocketJump Film School argues that we only notice bad CG while great CG is invisible, so CG seems to be everywhere ruining movies when it often is not.
why_hn: Used as a counterpoint whenever commenters claim CGI always looks fake.

title: How Not to Land an Orbital Rocket Booster
summary: SpaceX's own compilation of failed orbital booster landing attempts, set to sound, showing the crashes before landings succeeded.
why_hn: HN uses it as evidence that SpaceX iterated through visible failures and is open and humorous about them.

title: I sent robot forgeries to a handwriting expert
summary: Stuff Made Here builds a handwriting robot and sends its output to a handwriting expert to see whether it can pass as forgery. It walks through the engineering trials and errors along the way.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as the physical-machine take on replicating handwriting, with plenty of explained iteration.

title: Are Crows the Ultimate Problem Solvers? | Inside the Animal Mind | BBC Earth
summary: A BBC Earth clip from Inside the Animal Mind in which a crow named 007 solves an eight-step puzzle to get a reward. It showcases crow problem-solving.
why_hn: Shared in crow-intelligence threads as a striking demonstration that changes how people see crows.

title: Climate Change Debate: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
summary: A short Last Week Tonight segment where John Oliver stages a statistically representative climate debate, with Bill Nye facing a crowd of dissenters. It satirizes false balance in media coverage.
why_hn: Cited to illustrate false balance and the trouble with giving all sides equal weight.

title: The 5 Most Dangerous Chemicals on Earth
summary: A SciShow episode in which Hank Green introduces five of the most dangerous chemicals, from lethal toxins to substances that explode on contact. It is an entertaining overview of extreme chemical hazards.
why_hn: Recommended as a fun companion to threads about hazardous chemistry, such as hydrofluoric acid and reactive substances.

title: A walk through of installing Synapse+Riot+Jitsi from scratch on Debian
summary: A walkthrough of installing Synapse, Riot and Jitsi from scratch on Debian to run your own Matrix communication service. The description warns it is now quite outdated and links to updated material.
why_hn: Recommended as a practical demonstration that self-hosting a Matrix server is fairly easy, even on a small droplet.

title: Why are we changing maps?  (from The West Wing)
summary: A short clip from The West Wing in which staffers meet a group advocating the Peters projection and challenge the Mercator map. It was shown as geography humor at a Salt Lake GIS user group meeting.
why_hn: HN links it in any thread on map projections and the Mercator distortion of country sizes, often calling it a favorite scene.

title: First Follower: Leadership Lessons from Dancing Guy
summary: Derek Sivers annotates a short clip of a lone dancer at a festival, showing how a first follower turns a ridiculous act into a movement. He draws out lessons about leadership and making it easy to follow.
why_hn: A go-to short explanation of how movements start and why early followers matter.

title: Disney's Practical Guide to Path Tracing
summary: Walt Disney Animation Studios' short introduction to path tracing, showing how rays are traced and bounced through a virtual scene to simulate light. It explains how this approach is used in animated films.
why_hn: Recommended as an approachable intro to path tracing in ray tracing and rendering threads.

title: Why Spotify Will Ultimately Fail
summary: Benn Jordan argues that Spotify's business model undermines the music it sells, using streaming payout figures and the economics for artists and labels.
why_hn: Commenters recommend it as an artist's informed explanation of streaming economics and why Spotify pays so little compared with alternatives like Bandcamp.

title: OODA Loop & Evolutionary Epistemology of John Boyd by Chuck Spinney
summary: Chuck Spinney, a long-time associate of John Boyd, presents Boyd's thinking on the OODA loop and evolutionary epistemology. The talk runs about two and a half hours and includes Q&A.
why_hn: HN readers recommend it as the way to learn what Boyd actually meant by OODA, straight from a collaborator, rather than from the popularized loop diagram.

title: Gil Scott-Heron - Whitey On the Moon (Official Audio)
summary: Gil Scott-Heron's 1970 spoken-word piece, in an official audio upload. It contrasts the Apollo moon program with poverty and neglect at home.
why_hn: Posted in space-spending threads as a classic critique of priorities, usually with a quip.

title: ADHD & How Anyone Can Improve Their Focus
summary: Andrew Huberman discusses ADHD, its biology and myths, behavioral and pharmacologic treatments, and training protocols to improve focus for people with or without ADHD. It covers dopamine and the coordination of brain networks.
why_hn: HN people offer it as practical focus and ADHD advice from a credentialed neuroscientist, though some treat it as only a reference.

title: Consciousness is Not a Computation (Roger Penrose) | AI Podcast Clips
summary: Clip from Lex Fridman's podcast with Roger Penrose in which Penrose argues that consciousness is not a computation. He discusses Godel-style arguments and the possible role of quantum effects in microtubules.
why_hn: Pointed to in consciousness and AI threads as the best-known statement of Penrose's view, which commenters find interesting even when they disagree.

title: Category Theory in Life - Eugenia Cheng
summary: Eugenia Cheng gives the opening keynote at Lambda World 2017, presenting category theory as very abstract algebra whose abstraction gives it broad applicability. She applies it to everyday questions including privilege and prejudice.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an accessible, gentle introduction that makes category theory feel approachable and shows its analogy-making power.

title: Birth of The Transistor: A video history of Japan's electronic industry. (Part 1)
summary: First part of a four-part video history of Japan's electronics industry, covering the birth of the transistor and the rise of Japanese semiconductors. It appears to draw on NHK documentary material.
why_hn: Recommended in documentary and semiconductor-history threads as a detailed look at Japan's chip industry.

title: Bach, Toccata and Fugue in D minor, organ
summary: Bach's Toccata and Fugue in D minor on organ, shown with a Music Animation Machine bar-graph score instead of traditional notation.
why_hn: Recommended as a music visualization that makes the structure easier to follow than sheet music.

title: How American Fire Departments are Getting People Killed
summary: Not Just Bikes argues that oversized American fire trucks and fire department requirements push cities toward wide roads and dangerous street design. He compares this with the Dutch approach to emergency response.
why_hn: HN people link it in threads on big vehicles and road safety as a comparison of US and Dutch fire department approaches.

title: Renting vs. Buying a Home: What People Get Wrong
summary: Ben Felix argues that common beliefs about renting versus buying are wrong: homes are not great investments, mortgages are not a wealth hack, and ownership does not reliably bring happiness.
why_hn: Recommended as detailed math on rent versus buy, showing the choice is often roughly a wash.

title: I tried using AI. It scared me.
